summary: This informational document describes the Argon2 memory-hard function for password hashing and proof-of-work, with an implementer-oriented description and test vectors. It is a product of the CFRG in the IRTF and aims to simplify adoption of Argon2 in Internet protocols.

plainLanguage.summary: Storing passwords safely means scrambling them in a way that is slow and memory hungry for thieves. Argon2 is such a scrambler, and this document explains it.

subtitle: A password hashing function that is deliberately hungry for memory, so attackers cannot cheaply guess at scale.

tldr.problem: Passwords and keys derived from them need a hash that is expensive to brute-force, including on specialised hardware, and the original Argon2 design needed an implementer-oriented description for Internet protocols.
tldr.mechanism: Argon2 fills a large block of memory using the BLAKE2b-based hash, then makes further passes over it, so that each guess costs memory as well as time. It has three variants: Argon2d, Argon2i and Argon2id.
tldr.outcome: The RFC gives the algorithm, recommended parameter choices and test vectors. Argon2id MUST be supported, and two settings are named as the first and second recommended options.

today: RFC 9106 is an Informational document from the IRTF. The unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it, so it remains the RFC description of Argon2.

sections.title: What Argon2 Is For
sections.content:
RFC 9106 describes Argon2, a memory-hard function for password hashing and proof-of-work applications. It gives an implementer-oriented description with test vectors, and corresponds to version 1.3 of the Argon2 hash function. It is a product of the Crypto Forum Research Group (CFRG) in the IRTF, and it is not an Internet Standards Track document.

Argon2 has one primary variant, Argon2id, and two supplementary variants. Argon2d uses data-dependent memory access, which suits cryptocurrencies and proof-of-work where side-channel timing attacks are not a threat. Argon2i uses data-independent memory access, which is preferred for password hashing and password-based key derivation. Argon2id works as Argon2i for the first half of the first pass and as Argon2d for the rest.

Argon2id MUST be supported by any implementation of this document, whereas Argon2d and Argon2i MAY be supported.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three flavours of the same recipe. One is best against cheaters who can only watch from far away, one is best against sneaky peekers, and the third mixes both. The mixed one is the one everybody must make.

sections.title: Inputs and Outputs
sections.content:
Argon2 takes these inputs: a message string P (the password), a nonce S (the salt), a degree of parallelism p, a tag length T, a memory size m in kibibytes, a number of passes t, a version number v (one byte, 0x13), an optional secret value K, optional associated data X and a type y. The type is 0 for Argon2d, 1 for Argon2i and 2 for Argon2id.

The salt is RECOMMENDED to be 16 bytes for password hashing and SHOULD be unique for each password. The degree of parallelism is an integer from 1 to 2^(24)-1, and the tag length is an integer number of bytes from 4 to 2^(32)-1. The memory size runs from 8*p to 2^(32)-1 kibibytes. The output, called the tag, is a string T bytes long.
sections.plainLanguage: You give Argon2 the password, a bit of random seasoning (the salt), and settings for how much desk space, how many rounds and how many helpers to use. You get back a scrambled string of the length you asked for.

sections.title: How the Memory Is Filled
sections.content:
Argon2 first hashes all inputs into a 64-byte value H_0, using BLAKE2b. It then allocates memory as m' blocks of 1024 bytes, arranged as a matrix with p rows (lanes). The first two blocks of each lane come from H_0. Every later block is computed by the compression function G from the previous block in the lane and a reference block chosen elsewhere in memory.

If there is more than one pass, the passes after the first repeat the computation, but each new value is XORed with the old one. After all passes, the last column of blocks is XORed together into a final block, and the output tag is derived from that block with the variable-length hash function H'.

To allow parallel work, memory is split into 4 vertical slices. The intersection of a slice and a lane is a segment, and segments of the same slice can be computed in parallel. How the reference block is picked is what separates the variants. Argon2d takes it from the content of the previous block. Argon2i derives it from the pass, lane, slice and other counters. Argon2id uses the Argon2i method in pass 0 for slices 0 and 1, and the Argon2d method after that.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine filling a huge grid of boxes, where each new box is a mix of the box before it and some other earlier box. To check the final answer you have to keep the whole grid around, which is what makes guessing expensive.

sections.title: The Compression Function and Permutation
sections.content:
The compression function G(X, Y) works on two 1024-byte blocks. It XORs them into R, views R as an 8x8 matrix of 16-byte registers, applies the permutation P to each row and then to each column, and outputs the result XORed with R.

Permutation P is based on the round function of BLAKE2b. The one difference is that the modular additions are combined with 64-bit multiplications. The RFC says this choice is meant to increase circuit depth, and so the running time of ASIC implementations, while keeping roughly the same running time on CPUs thanks to parallelism and pipelining.
sections.plainLanguage: Two big boxes of numbers get stirred together, first row by row and then column by column. The stirring uses multiplication, which is easy for a normal computer but awkward for a custom cracking machine.

sections.title: Choosing Parameters
sections.content:
The RFC gives a procedure for choosing the type and parameters. If a uniformly safe option is acceptable, the first recommended option is Argon2id with t=1 iteration, p=4 lanes, m=2^(21) (2 GiB of RAM), a 128-bit salt and a 256-bit tag. If much less memory is available, the second recommended option is Argon2id with t=3 iterations, p=4 lanes, m=2^(16) (64 MiB of RAM), a 128-bit salt and a 256-bit tag.

Otherwise, start by choosing the type (Argon2id if you do not know the difference or consider side-channel attacks a viable threat), use p=4 lanes, work out the memory and time each call can afford, and raise the number of passes t as far as the time budget allows. A 128-bit salt is sufficient for all applications, and a 128-bit tag is sufficient for most, including key derivation.
sections.plainLanguage: If you do not know what settings to pick, the RFC hands you two ready-made recipes: a big one for roomy computers and a smaller one for tight spaces.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The collision and preimage resistance of Argon2 match those of the underlying BLAKE2b hash. The RFC then discusses time-space trade-off attacks, which compute the function while storing fewer blocks at the cost of more computation. For example, the best known attack on 1-pass and 2-pass Argon2i reduces the time-area product by a factor of 5, and the best trade-off attack on t-pass Argon2d reduces it by a factor of 1.33.

For time-bounded defenders, the RFC notes that 3 passes is almost optimal for Argon2i, while 1 pass maximizes attack costs for Argon2d and Argon2id. Its recommendation is that Argon2id with t=1 and 2 GiB of memory be the default for all environments, and Argon2id with t=3 and 64 MiB of memory be the default for memory-constrained environments. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: Clever cheaters might try to use less desk space and do more work instead. The authors studied the best tricks and picked settings that keep those tricks from helping much.
